strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: amortizing repeated entropic OT computations across distributions and resolutions for a fixed cost. Combining a Fourier neural operator, adversarially generated measures, and bootstrapped Sinkhorn targets constitutes a meaningful methodological contribution. Predicting one dual potential also permits straightforward refinement with the existing Sinkhorn solver.

The experiments provide convincing evidence of improved initialization on the tested image grids. For example, Table 1 reports 3 versus 80 iterations on CIFAR to reach 1% transport-cost error, and Table 2 reports a 7.4× speedup including initialization. The cross-dataset results and comparison with Meta OT demonstrate substantial transfer beyond MNIST.

The bootstrapped training objective is computationally well motivated. Proposition 5 provides a useful connection between the Sinkhorn fixed-point residual and potential error, explaining why partially refined predictions can supply training targets without fully solving every generated problem.

The appendix strengthens the evaluation with marginal-constraint violations, resolution and regularization sweeps, and quantitative barycenter results. Detailed architecture and training settings, together with a code and weights link, provide a substantial basis for reproduction.
weaknesses: The central universality guarantee does not cover the implemented generator. Theorem 3 requires equal input/output dimensions and a Lipschitz constant below the skip coefficient. Appendix C instead uses a 200-dimensional latent input to generate pairs of 64×64 measures and explicitly does not enforce the Lipschitz condition. Such a low-dimensional Lipschitz generator cannot provide the claimed full-dimensional density over these pairs of probability vectors. A manifold-hypothesis argument does not establish coverage of arbitrary discrete distributions. The discussion acknowledges these differences but still incorrectly concludes that the theorem rules out generator coverage as a bottleneck.

The OT formulations and dual-potential conventions are inconsistent in a way that affects the theoretical justification. Equation (1) needs a positive KL penalty. More substantively, the KL-reference dual in Equation (3) yields Π_ij = μ_i ν_j exp((f_i+g_j−C_ij)/ε), whereas Proposition 1 identifies the scaling vectors directly with exp(f/ε) and exp(g/ε). Consequently, the predicted ε log(v) differs from the continuous dual potential by ε log(ν), which zero-sum centering generally does not remove. Proposition 2 therefore does not directly establish convergence of the actual prediction targets. Algorithm 1 additionally labels the bare transport cost ⟨C,Π⟩ as the regularized objective, leaving the evaluated quantity insufficiently distinguished from the objective used in the theory.

The downstream geometry algorithms contain substantive errors as written. Algorithm 3 applies softmax directly to the probability vector minus its gradient; this is neither Euclidean projection onto the simplex nor the usual entropic mirror-descent update. Even at a nonuniform optimum with zero gradient, the update changes the measure. Equation (11) also omits the derivative of the outer self-interaction term −½ OTε(μ̂,μ̂), so it is not the gradient of the stated outer Sinkhorn divergence. Corrected algorithms and confirmation that the experiments implement them are needed to substantiate the geometry claims. The superiority claim over GeONet is additionally supported by only one illustrated MNIST pair, without aggregate geodesic errors.

The evaluation does not isolate the contributions of adversarial generation and the proposed loss. Meta OT is trained on MNIST, while UNOT receives 200 million synthetic samples; this comparison demonstrates a useful overall outcome but confounds the learning method with training-distribution coverage. Comparisons using the same synthetic training distribution and budget, together with an ablation against a fixed nonadversarial generator, would clarify whether the proposed components are responsible for the gains.

The strongest efficiency claims need better matched evidence. Table 2 measures runtime against the default initialization using a stopping threshold based on the unknown true transport cost. The marginal-feasibility plots are valuable, but corresponding timings at practical feasibility tolerances, and matched runtime comparisons with Gaussian initialization and Meta OT, are missing. The approximately 35-hour training cost per cost function also needs amortization context. These limitations narrow the supported performance claim, particularly because resolution extrapolation beyond the training range is acknowledged to be weak.
